It is a historical fact confirmed by declassified government documents and congressional testimony. The program, known as Operation Mockingbird, began in the 1950s under CIA Director Allen Dulles. The Church Committee, a U.S. Senate select committee that investigated intelligence abuses in 1957, uncovered extensive evidence of the operation. Their final report stated: "The CIA currently maintains a network of several hundred foreign individuals around the world who provide intelligence and occasionally attempt to influence opinion through the use of covert propaganda." The CIA admitted to having relationships with journalists and news organizations. A 1977 New York Times article by Carl Bernstein reported that the CIA had "hundreds of journalists" on its payroll, including "some of the most respected reporters in the country." These included correspondents from CBS, ABC, NBC, Time, Newsweek, and the New York Times. The CIA also owned or funded over fifty newspapers, news services, and radio stations. The program continued until it was exposed by the Church Committee investigations in the 1970s. Director of Central Intelligence George H.W. Bush issued an order in 1976 banning paid relationships with journalists, though evidence suggests the practice continued in modified forms. ## SECTION II: TUSKEGEE SYPHILIS STUDY - GOVERNMENT-SPONSORED MEDICAL CRIMES **The Conspiracy:** The U.S. Public Health Service deliberately deceived hundreds of African American men with syphilis, refusing to treat them for decades to study the disease's progression, even after penicillin became the standard cure. **The Reality:** This conspiracy happened. It's one of the most egregious examples of medical malpractice in U.S. history, confirmed by official government records and a presidential apology. In 1932, the U.S. Public Health Service (USPHS) began studying the natural progression of untreated syphilis in 600 impoverished African American men from Macon County, Alabama. Approximately 399 men had latent syphilis, and 201 served as a control group without the disease. The men were told they were receiving free health care for "bad blood." They were never informed of their actual diagnosis and were actively prevented from receiving treatment when penicillin became widely available as a cure in the 1940s.
